e: Plain English Words this page uses because the court uses them. Nothing here is special to this case. The paperwork How a case moves The ones that can end it The test this case turned on

Plymouth County Superior Court, Massachusetts · No. 2383CR00199 Commonwealth v. Clancy A first‑degree murder prosecution in which the defense disputed almost none of what happened, and contested only whether the defendant was criminally responsible for it. Outside the courtroom it was argued at enormous volume on TikTok and other similar platforms. People claimed to see a gender divide in how much sympathy Clancy was owed, and before long that claim was being argued about as much as the case. Inside the courtroom, after seven days, the jury could not agree, and on September 4, 2026, the judge declared a mistrial. Nothing was decided. Indicted Sept 15, 2023 Before Sullivan, J. Tried Jul 20 – Sept 4, 2026 Status Mistrial

Prosecution The side bringing the charges The state of Massachusetts Nobody sues in a criminal case. The state brings the charges, and Massachusetts calls itself the Commonwealth, so that’s the name on the case. The lawyers doing it work for the Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office, which prosecutes crimes across the county south of Boston that Duxbury is in. Timothy Cruz has been the district attorney there since 2001. Background: Plymouth County District Attorney

Defendant The person charged Labor and delivery nurse Before any of this she was a labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, so her job was looking after women giving birth. She was in her early thirties and lived with her family in Duxbury, a coastal town south of Boston, where she was raising three young children. She wasn’t a public figure. What most people know about her, they know from this case. Reporting: CBS Boston, Oct 24, 2023
Notes This case is live and this page will go out of date. Record reviewed through November 8, 2026 , six days after the double jeopardy motion was argued. The next hearing is November 16, 2026 .
How this was made, and what it leaves out

Built from the 299 pages of search warrant affidavits unsealed in October 2023, the emergency petition to the Supreme Judicial Court of September 4, 2026, the Massachusetts model jury instruction on criminal responsibility, and transcripts of the televised trial. A caution about those transcripts. They are transcripts of the broadcast, not of the court reporter, so they carry no page and line numbers — citations here are to the trial day, which is why they look unlike the citations on the other pages in this series. They also misspell names, including the judge’s. Every name on this page has been checked against something other than the transcript. Dates and rulings outside those documents come from the district attorney’s press releases and from news reporting. Every citation with a public copy links to it, and anything taken from coverage is marked as reporting. The court’s own orders in this case are not published online, so a ruling is cited to the coverage of it.

Sealed throughout: the defendant’s medical and psychiatric records beyond what was put in evidence, and material concerning the surviving family. Parts of the expert litigation were heard in camera. Since September 14, 2026, the juror list has been impounded indefinitely, after the identity of the holdout juror was circulated online.

Three children died, ages five, three and eight months. They are named in the public record; they are named here once, in the entry for the day it happened, and are not used as illustration anywhere else on the page. The clinical and forensic detail in the medical testimony is cited and summarized, not reproduced. That is a deliberate limit and it costs the page something: readers who want that detail will have to go to the record for it.

Not legal advice, not a finding, and not a verdict — here least of all. A mistrial decides nothing. It leaves the charges live, the defendant presumed innocent of them, and every contested question exactly where it stood before the trial began. This page does not supply the answer the jury declined to give. The volume of opinion outside the courtroom did not supply it either, and neither does the reporting of an eleven-to-one split: under the law an eleven-to-one split is not a verdict, and a juror who will not join eleven others has done nothing wrong by refusing.
The court’s numbered list of everything filed in a case. Entry 42 is the forty-second thing filed.
The formal charge that starts a felony case in the Superior Court. It replaces the complaint the district court began with.
One charged offense. This case went to the jury on three of them, and a jury answers for each one separately.
A jury that decides only whether there is enough evidence to charge someone, not whether they are guilty. It hears one side.
The word-for-word record of a proceeding. A court reporter’s transcript is cited by page and line; a transcript of a televised proceeding, as here, has no line numbers and is cited by day.
A document, object or record put in evidence. This trial had roughly three hundred.
Filed with the court but kept off the public record. Both sides and the judge can read it; nobody else can. Material is unsealed when that is lifted, as the search warrants were in October 2023.
Withheld from public inspection by order. The juror list in this case was impounded indefinitely after the trial.
A sworn written statement. A search warrant affidavit is the officer’s account of why there is reason to search. It is not evidence at trial.
The hearing where the charges are read and the defendant pleads. It happens once in the district court and again after indictment.
A formal request that the court do something. The other side files an opposition; the moving side may then file a reply.
To agree formally that something is true so it need not be proved. The other side does not have to accept the offer, and here it did not.
Heard in private, in the judge’s chambers rather than in open court.
Evidence one side puts in to answer the other’s case, after that case has closed. It cannot open new ground.
An appeal taken in the middle of a case rather than at the end of it. They are rare, and usually urgent.
Argued, but not yet decided. The judge will rule later.
A trial ended without a verdict. It decides nothing: the charges stay live and the case can, in principle, be tried again.
A jury that cannot reach the required unanimity. Eleven to one is not a verdict, and is worth no more than nothing to one.
What a Massachusetts judge tells a deadlocked jury: reconsider, but surrender no conscientiously held belief. Elsewhere it is called an Allen charge, or a dynamite charge.
A motion asking the judge to enter a finding of not guilty because no rational juror could convict on the evidence. It is about legal sufficiency, not about whether this jury was persuaded.
The rule against being tried twice for the same offense. A mistrial usually does not trigger it, which is why it has to be argued.
The standard a judge must meet to end a trial without a verdict over the defendant’s objection. If it was not met, a second trial is barred.
Which side has to prove a thing. If they do not, they lose that point, even if the other side proves nothing either.
The criminal standard, and the highest one the law uses. It is not proof beyond all possible doubt.
One of the separate things the prosecution has to prove for a particular crime. If one is missing, the charge fails.
Whether the defendant can be held answerable at all. In Massachusetts the Commonwealth must prove she was responsible, beyond a reasonable doubt. The defendant proves nothing.
A legal term, not a medical one. It need not match any formal diagnosis, and a jury decides whether there was one.

The second prong. Even with a mental disease or defect, a person is responsible if she could both appreciate that what she was doing was wrong and conform her conduct to the law. Losing either is enough.
To understand, rather than merely to know. Knowing an act is illegal is not the same as grasping what that means.
Not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility
Often shortened to NGI. It is not an acquittal in effect: it ordinarily leads to a petition to commit, and commitment is reviewed at intervals and renewable without limit.
A court order holding a person in a hospital for treatment, not as a punishment. It is reviewed at intervals and can be renewed.
A rare and serious illness arising after childbirth. It is a clinical term and carries no legal consequence by itself — the legal test is the one above.

Where it stands No verdict. The jury could not agree, and a mistrial was declared on September 4, 2026. Whether she can be tried again was argued on November 2, and the judge hasn’t ruled. If yes If proved If not proved If the jury cannot agree The burden runs the opposite way to the intuition: the Commonwealth had to prove she was responsible, not the defense that she was not. Nothing on this diagram asks whether she killed her children, because by the time the jury was empaneled nobody was arguing about it.
Did the Commonwealth prove the elements of murder?

Whose burden is it? The Commonwealth’s Not in dispute A burden is the job of proving something, so before anything else it matters whose job that is. Here it’s entirely the Commonwealth’s, which is what Massachusetts calls the prosecution. They have to prove two things, which are this question and the one under it, and they have to prove both beyond a reasonable doubt, the highest standard the law has. She doesn’t have to prove anything, and that includes proving she was insane. The judge told the jury so in these words: “The defendant has no burden to prove a lack of criminal responsibility.” This is the part most arguments about the case get backwards. People assume it was on her to prove she was insane. It was on them to prove she was criminally responsible. Elements are the separate pieces a crime is made of, and the prosecution has to prove every one of them. In most murder trials this is the whole fight. In this one it wasn’t a fight at all. The defense didn’t dispute what she did. They even offered to stipulate to it, which means formally agreeing something is true so that nobody has to prove it. The Commonwealth turned that offer down and put the evidence in front of the jury anyway. So this step is marked as not in dispute, and the real argument is all in the second thing they had to prove.
Did the Commonwealth prove she was criminally responsible?

The jury stopped here No verdict Criminal responsibility is the legal name for what most people would call the insanity question. It asks if she can be held answerable for what she did, given the state of her mind that day. This is the only thing the two sides really fought over. The trial ran for about six weeks and nearly all of the evidence went to this. The Commonwealth said she was severely depressed but not psychotic, and that she made a series of deliberate choices. The defense said she was in postpartum psychosis. To prove she was responsible, the Commonwealth had two ways of doing it, which are the two cards inside this one. This is also as far as the jury got. They couldn’t agree on it, and that’s why it says no verdict. Whichever way they try, it has to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. That doesn’t mean beyond every possible doubt, but it’s a long way past “probably.” And all twelve jurors have to agree on the answer, whichever answer it is. A yes on either one is enough or
Was she free of any mental disease or defect?

This is the first way the Commonwealth could prove she was criminally responsible. They could show that at the time of the killings she had no mental disease or defect at all. That phrase is a legal one, not a medical one. It doesn’t have to match any official diagnosis, and it’s the jury that decides if she had one, not the doctors. If the Commonwealth proved this, that was enough, and the other question in this card wouldn’t matter.
If she had one, did she keep substantial capacity?

This is the second way, in case the jury thought she did have a mental disease or defect. Having one doesn’t make a person not responsible all by itself. The Commonwealth could still succeed by proving she kept what the law calls substantial capacity, and that has two parts. One is that she could appreciate that what she was doing was wrong. The other is that she was able to make herself follow the law. They had to prove she kept both. If her illness took away either one, she isn’t responsible. And “appreciate” is a stronger word than “know.” It means really understanding that something is wrong, not just being aware that it’s illegal.

Yes Then the jury reaches the counts Four ways it can land If the jury had found she was criminally responsible, they still wouldn’t have been done. That finding only opens the door to the actual charges, which were three counts of first-degree murder. On those the jury would have had four options, which were first-degree murder, second-degree murder, manslaughter, or not guilty. This is the only point where the evidence about what she did, and how, would really start to matter, because that’s what separates one of those options from the next.

No Then the verdict is Not guilty by reason of insanity If the Commonwealth didn’t prove she was criminally responsible, the verdict is not guilty by reason of insanity. A lot of people hear that as walking free, and it isn’t. What generally happens next is that the district attorney asks the court to commit her, which means ordering her held in a mental health facility or at Bridgewater State Hospital. A commitment gets reviewed every so often, but it can be renewed again and again with no limit, for as long as she is still ill and still dangerous. The judge told the jury it could last for the rest of her life.
Neither. The jury never answered the question

What actually happened Then A mistrial, declared on September 4, 2026 This is what actually happened, and it’s neither of the two endings that question leads to. The jury deliberated for thirty-eight hours over seven days and sent the judge three notes. They ended up split eleven to one. A verdict has to be unanimous, so eleven to one counts for exactly as much as no agreement at all. That’s called a hung jury. On September 4, 2026, the judge declared a mistrial, which is a trial that ends without a verdict. A mistrial decides nothing. She wasn’t found guilty and she wasn’t found not guilty. The charges are still there and the case can be tried again in front of a new jury. The defense has asked the court to rule that a second trial isn’t allowed. That was argued on November 2, 2026. The judge hasn’t ruled yet, and the next hearing is November 16.
None of this is disputed. The defense has never contested any of it — which is what makes the rest of the case unusual.

Lindsay Clancy, a labor and delivery nurse in her early thirties, is under treatment for anxiety and insomnia that began after the birth of her third child. Over some five months she is seen by a psychiatrist and a psychiatric nurse practitioner, is briefly hospitalized, and is moved through a succession of medications. She keeps notebooks throughout, tracking doses and symptoms. The warrant affidavits describe them as documenting “her mental state and her feelings about her children, in addition to keeping track of her medications.” At trial the defense used the handwriting itself as evidence: legible in November, close to illegible by January. Search warrant affidavits, unsealed Oct 2023, at p. 105

A virtual appointment with her psychiatrist. She denies both suicidal and homicidal thoughts. The Commonwealth would return to this exchange repeatedly; so would the defense, for opposite reasons. Her psychiatrist testified that her mood that day was depressed and her affect “depressed and flat,” that she saw no sign of psychosis, and that Clancy answered no when asked about suicidal or homicidal thoughts. The plan was to slow the Valium taper and raise the amitriptyline to 20 milligrams. On cross she agreed she had not recommended a hospital evaluation. Asked whether the higher dose “pushed her over the edge,” she answered, “I don’t think so.” Tr. Day 9, 4:44:24–4:49:06; Tr. Day 10, 2:59:07–3:01:43 and 3:37:43

In the course of an ordinary day — a pediatrician appointment, a snowman, art projects — Lindsay Clancy asks her husband to go out for takeout and a prescription. While he is gone she strangles their three children in the basement with exercise bands. Cora was five, Dawson three, Callan eight months. She then cuts her wrists and neck and goes out a second‑story window, sustaining spinal injuries that leave her paralyzed from the waist down. Her husband returns shortly after six and calls 911 at 6:11 p.m. Two of the children are pronounced dead that evening; the youngest is removed from life support three days later. Clancy later described a commanding male voice telling her it was her last chance. Whether that account is a symptom or a construction is, in the end, the entire case. The clinical and forensic detail is extensive and is in the public record. It is cited here and not reproduced.
Charges, and three years of paper
From the arrest warrant to the eve of trial. Almost all of it is argument about what a jury would be allowed to hear.

Two counts of murder, three of strangulation, three of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. A third murder count follows after the youngest child dies on January 27. The warrant issued out of Plymouth District Court the day after the deaths. The investigation was already running: the affidavits record a trooper attending the first autopsies at about nine that morning. By the arraignment on February 7 the complaint carried three counts each of murder, strangulation, and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Plymouth County District Attorney, press release of Feb 7, 2023; Search warrant affidavits at p. 105; reporting: WHDH, Jan 25, 2023

Plymouth District Court, by video link. She pleads not guilty. She has been in the hospital since the night of the killings and will not appear in a courtroom in person for a long time. Judge John Canavan presided, and she appeared over Zoom from a hospital bed in Boston. He ordered her held in a medical facility until her treatment was complete, with bail to be taken up after that. She was moved to Tewksbury State Hospital that May. Her first appearance in a courtroom in person came on February 20, 2026, three years later. Plymouth County District Attorney, press release of Feb 7, 2023; reporting: Duxbury Clipper, Nov 1, 2023; NBC10 Boston, Mar 2, 2026

A Plymouth County grand jury returns three counts of first‑degree murder and three of strangulation. The case moves to the Superior Court as No. 2383CR00199. The district attorney’s announcement gives the medical examiner’s findings: asphyxia for the two older children, and complications of asphyxia for the youngest. A psychiatrist retained by the Commonwealth had spoken to the grand jury. She was being held without bail in a medical facility. Plymouth County District Attorney, press release of Sept 15, 2023; reporting: Duxbury Clipper, Nov 1, 2023

The Superior Court arraignment is held at the hospital where she is being held. Not guilty again. Sullivan, J. presided, and the public could watch over Zoom. She sat in a wheelchair between Kevin Reddington and a psychiatrist retained by the defense. Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague appeared for the Commonwealth. The judge ordered that she stay at Tewksbury State Hospital, held without bail. Plymouth County District Attorney, press release of Oct 26, 2023; reporting: Duxbury Clipper, Nov 1, 2023

Eleven search warrants, applied for in the weeks after January, become public. They are the most substantial primary document in the case and the closest thing to a narrative the investigation ever filed. They also carry an assertion that six separate applications repeat word for word: that Clancy used her phone and journal for “researching ways to kill.” It appears each time as the premise for searching one more device. Nothing in the 299 pages establishes it, and at trial the Commonwealth’s own forensic examiner testified he had found no such searches. Search warrant affidavits ¶¶40, 42, repeated at pp. 105, 139, 173, 208, 236, 264; Tr. Day 13

The defense argues the Plymouth jury pool has been saturated by local coverage and asks for Suffolk. Denied: the judge finds a fair jury can be seated where the case arose. Decided at a hearing on November 18, 2025, which she attended by Zoom. At the same hearing the judge moved the trial from February 9 to July 20, 2026. It was the third postponement, and both sides agreed to it, calling the case “discovery intensive.” How she would be brought into a courtroom, in a wheelchair and from a hospital, was discussed and left open. Reporting: NBC10 Boston, Nov 18, 2025

Kevin Reddington files formal notice. From this point the case is not about what happened. The ground had been prepared well before the notice. In January 2025 the court had ordered her to be examined by the Commonwealth’s experts, and a further forensic evaluation was fixed for April 10 to 12, 2026. Early in 2026 a malpractice suit was filed in her name in Norfolk Superior Court, alleging that her providers failed to diagnose bipolar disorder and put her through a “disorganized, uncoordinated course of polypharmacy.” Reporting: NBC10 Boston, Jan 14, 2025; NBC10 Boston, Mar 2, 2026; NBC10 Boston, Mar 31, 2026
Two attempts to take the acts off the table

The defense asks first to split the trial in two — did she do it, then was she responsible — and then, when that fails, offers to stipulate in writing to her involvement in the deaths. The Commonwealth declines the stipulation and elects to put the evidence in. Bifurcation denied in an order reported on March 31, on the ground that the evidence and witnesses overlap almost entirely: “These are overlapping issues that do not require bifurcation.” The stipulation rejected April 22. Both rulings had the same practical effect: a jury deciding a question about her mind would first sit through weeks of evidence about the deaths of three children. Whether that was prejudice or simply the Commonwealth’s case is contested, and is one of the things the defense has continued to litigate since. Reporting: NBC10 Boston, Mar 2, 2026; NBC10 Boston, Mar 31, 2026; WHDH, Mar 31, 2026; Boston Globe, Apr 7, 2026; Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly, Apr 26, 2026

Days before the trial is due to start, the Commonwealth dismisses all three strangulation counts as duplicative of the murder counts. Three charges remain: first‑degree murder, three times. The district attorney’s office said the counts “would be subsumed into the murder charges indicted and are therefore redundant.” Around the same time the judge ruled that the jury could hear the 911 calls made after her husband found the children. Reporting: Boston 25 News, Jul 10, 2026
Six weeks, more than eighty witnesses, some three hundred exhibits — almost none of it directed at whether she did it.

Eighteen jurors seated, six of them alternates. Openings follow on July 27. Six alternates is a large number. The judge told the jurors why at the end: it was “a lengthy case over the summer.” On July 31 the jury was taken by bus along the route her husband drove that evening and then through the house in Duxbury, in groups of six. On August 4 she answered the judge’s questions about a stipulation covering the blood, the bands and the DNA, which spared the jury days of chain-of-custody witnesses. Tr. Closing Arguments, 2:50:38; reporting: ABC7, Aug 1, 2026; Boston.com, Aug 4, 2026

First responders, the scene, the medical examiner, the digital evidence, and then the clinicians who treated her. The through‑line is choice: that she selected the place, the method and the moment, and sent her husband out to create it. The treating clinicians are the heart of it. Her psychiatrist testified across two full days and the nurse practitioner for a third; neither had recorded observing psychosis, and both confirmed she had denied homicidal thoughts. The Commonwealth’s position is that the people who actually saw her, saw no psychosis. Tr. Days 9, 10, 11

The defense spends much of its cross‑examination not on the mental health evidence but on the quality of the police work: what was looked for, what was not, and how long it sat. The clearest example: a State Police forensic examiner agreed there were no “ways to kill” searches on the computer, and that he had not encountered any such searches attributable to either Clancy. The one suicide‑methods page in evidence was on the husband’s laptop, reached through a Wikipedia hyperlink in August 2022, five months before the deaths — and that laptop was not examined until 2025. Tr. Day 13

Family, the family’s nanny, and the experts. The account offered is of a woman misdiagnosed and over‑medicated by clinicians who never spoke to one another, whose psychosis was invisible to them because none of them was looking. The forensic psychiatrist called by the defense put it at its highest: that she was frankly psychotic that day, acting not out of malice but out of a suicidal conviction that the children could not survive without her. A second defense expert concluded she could neither appreciate the wrongfulness of the act nor conform her conduct to the law. Tr. Days 15, 16, 17, 18

Three forensic experts for the Commonwealth close the evidence. The core of it: a major depressive episode, yes — but no mania, no hypomania, and so no bipolar diagnosis and no psychosis. A voice heard once, they said, is not how psychosis usually presents. The last of the three told the jury it was unusual that she had never reported a voice to any clinician before that day, and “very unusual” that it stopped once the youngest child had been strangled. Asked whether it is typical in psychosis to hear a voice once, never before and never after, he answered no. When the Commonwealth rested, the judge agreed to put manslaughter to the jury and refused the defense’s request for an instruction on a faulty investigation. Tr. Day 20, 6:54:31 and 7:00:13; Tr. Day 21, 3:14:20 and 3:47:31

Sullivan, J. instructs the jury on criminal responsibility before the elements of the offense, and tells them the burden of proving it is the Commonwealth’s, beyond a reasonable doubt. The defendant, he says, has none. “The defendant has no burden to prove a lack of criminal responsibility.” He also instructs them on what a verdict of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility actually produces: a petition to commit, Bridgewater State Hospital, review at intervals, and commitment renewable without limit — possibly, he tells them, for the duration of her life. Tr. Closing Arguments, 07:36 and 12:10
Thirty‑eight hours of deliberation, three notes, and no verdict.

The twelve deliberating jurors are drawn at random from the eighteen. Five verdicts are available to them: first‑degree murder, second‑degree murder, manslaughter, not guilty, or not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility. The clerk drew the alternates at random, with the foreperson kept out of the draw. Nine women and three men were left to deliberate. There was a verdict slip for each child, with a box for every outcome, and the foreperson was to tick one, sign it and date it. Tr. Closing Arguments, 2:50:38 and 2:54:12; reporting: NBC News, Sept 2, 2026
Deadlocked, and told to keep going

On the fourth day the jury reports it cannot agree. On the fifth the judge delivers the Tuey‑Rodriguez charge, asking them to re‑examine their positions without surrendering any conscientiously held belief. The first report came about an hour into Tuesday, September 1, and the judge sent the jury back without the formal charge. That afternoon a woman was arrested outside the courthouse, accused of filming jurors as they left. She pleaded not guilty. The next morning the judge spoke to each juror and alternate one at a time before deliberations resumed. The second note came at about 2 p.m. A Massachusetts judge may send a deadlocked jury back only twice unless the jury itself agrees to go on, so a third report would end the trial. Reporting: NBC News, Sept 2, 2026; Tr. Mistrial, 18:43

The foreperson writes that one juror has acknowledged doubt but will not apply it as the law requires. The judge questions the jurors and declines either to remove the juror or to inquire further, citing the privacy of deliberations. The note came after lunch. The judge had each juror brought in and asked whether they could follow his instructions, and all said they could. He then read the reasonable-doubt instruction again. Reddington asked for the juror to be removed. The Commonwealth answered that there was “no way to determine what the deliberations are.” The judge said it was not proper for him “to side with one side or the other of the deliberations.” The next morning he refused a further inquiry. Read strictly, he said, the note “does not indicate that this is a person who has refused to follow the law.” Reporting: NBC News, Sept 3, 2026; Tr. Mistrial, 07:23–10:00
An hour at the Supreme Judicial Court

With a mistrial about to be declared, the judge grants a one‑hour stay for an emergency interlocutory appeal. The defense petitions the SJC as No. SJ‑2026‑0402, asking it to order the trial court to examine the juror. A single justice denies it. The petition argues that a juror’s refusal to follow the law is never protected by the privacy of deliberations, and that this juror’s stated reasoning disclosed a bias against the mentally ill. Filed inside the hour, it prints the docket number a digit short. Emergency request for relief, SJ‑2026‑0402, citing Commonwealth v. Swafford, 441 Mass. 329 (2004); Tr. Mistrial, 24:02–26:40

A third note. Thirty‑eight hours over seven days, and no unanimity. The judge discharges the jury. Nothing is decided: the charges stand, and she is presumed innocent of them. The note read: “It is with a heavy heart that we report we are unable to come to a unanimous decision and will not be able to.” The Commonwealth said a mistrial was now required. Reddington asked first for the jury to be sent back once more, then for it to be polled on any charge it had agreed on, citing the Karen Read decision. The judge refused both: “I don’t feel I have any choice but to declare a mistrial at this time.” The clerk continued the case to September 29. Tr. Mistrial, 18:08, 19:37, 20:08 and 37:08; reporting: WBUR, Sept 4, 2026
Where the docket actually is, rather than where the coverage left it.
The jurors talk, and the juror list is sealed

Several jurors describe the deliberations publicly; the holdout gives his own account and disputes theirs. On September 14 the judge impounds the juror list indefinitely after the holdout is identified online. These accounts are not evidence and are not on the docket. They are here because the motions now pending turn on what happened in that room, and because the accounts conflict: the foreperson says the holdout acknowledged reasonable doubt and would not return the verdict it pointed to; the holdout says he had no doubt at all. Reporting: PBS News, Sept 28, 2026
Three motions, none of them a retrial

The defense moves under Rule 25 for a finding of not guilty on the ground the evidence was legally insufficient; separately to dismiss on double jeopardy; and separately again for further questioning of the holdout juror. The juror motion came first, around September 18. It asks the court to preserve the questionnaires, courthouse video and phone sign-in sheets for all eighteen jurors, and to make a “limited inquiry” into the holdout, including his phone records for each day of deliberations. The double jeopardy motion followed on September 21 from co-counsel Martin Weinberg. It argues there was no “manifest necessity” for a mistrial, “given the absence of judicial inquiry regarding repeated reports” about one juror. The Commonwealth filed a motion of its own, for an order limiting what Reddington says in public. WBZ and the Boston Globe opposed it. Reporting: Fox News, Sept 21, 2026; CBS Boston, Sept 29, 2026

Reddington argues the Rule 25 motion, attacking the exercise bands, the DNA, the fingerprint work and the investigation. It is taken under advisement. No retrial date is set. The next hearing is November 2; the district attorney has not said whether he will try the case again. Only the Rule 25 motion was argued. Reddington said there was a “total and complete lack of evidence.” Shanan Buckingham, for the Commonwealth, answered that this was the first time the defense had questioned the evidence that she did it. The double jeopardy motion, the juror motion and the Commonwealth’s request for a gag order were all put over to November 2. A lawyer appeared for the holdout, who is “Juror Doe” in the filings. The judge said his goal was to have the case tried “as soon as possible.” Reddington said he could not try it before June. Afterward the district attorney said his office was preparing as if a second trial were coming but had not decided. Reporting: CBS Boston, Sept 29, 2026

In a five‑page order the judge holds that the evidence was enough for a jury to convict. The first of the three motions is gone, and the other two are still to be argued. He wrote that the evidence would “permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder,” and that “there was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial.” Whether she could appreciate the wrongfulness of what she did was a question for a jury, he held, because the experts disagreed. The order does not find her responsible. It decides only that the question was properly a jury’s. Reporting: ABC News, Oct 1, 2026; CBS Boston, Oct 1, 2026; PBS News, Oct 1, 2026
No more questions for the holdout

The judge refuses to bring the holdout juror back for questioning, or to hold a hearing on whether he lied on his juror questionnaire. What came out after the mistrial, he writes, “simply is not relevant to whether there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial.” “Any further judicial inquiry is inappropriate,” he wrote. He leaned on the Karen Read decision, which warned that letting jurors’ accounts from after a trial count would cause “endless confusion and controversy.” So the November 2 hearing went ahead on the motion to dismiss without new evidence. The juror has denied lying on his form. Reporting: ABC News, Oct 21, 2026; NBC10 Boston, Oct 22, 2026

Weinberg argues the mistrial wasn’t necessary, because the judge didn’t look further into the notes about one juror. The judge rules on nothing from the bench. He sets another hearing for November 16 and suggests a retrial could start in March 2027. Weinberg said that after the foreperson’s two notes, saying a juror wasn’t following the rules, the judge should have questioned the foreperson separately. That might have turned up grounds to replace the holdout and let the jury keep going. Jennifer Sprague, for the Commonwealth, said going further would have meant reaching into the deliberations themselves, and that the judge had questioned the jurors and believed them. “This juror did not refuse to deliberate,” she said. “He refused to agree.” Reddington pressed again about the holdout’s phone and his answers at jury selection, and asked for his jury-service records. He said the juror’s name in open court, against the judge’s order, until the judge called a sidebar: “Why don’t we all dial this back a little bit.” The holdout’s lawyer, Heather O’Connor, said the defense had accepted him before trial and turned on him only once he held out: “We are here because Juror Doe did not vote the way that the defense needed.” The gag order request was argued too, and the defense calls it unconstitutional. The Commonwealth says it will try her again if it can, but hasn’t decided whether on the same charges. In September Reddington said he couldn’t be ready before June. Now he asked for a trial “this spring,” before this judge, who has to retire at 70 in June 2027. Reporting: AP, Nov 2, 2026; Boston.com, Nov 2, 2026; WBUR, Nov 2, 2026

Three counts of first‑degree murder, undecided. A defendant presumed innocent of them. The motion that could end the case without a second trial was argued on November 2, with a request for the holdout juror’s jury-service records and the gag order request, and the judge has ruled on none of them. He had already refused, on October 21, to bring the holdout back for questioning. The next hearing is November 16. If the case goes on, he has suggested a retrial in March 2027. This entry is the honest end of the page, and it will change.

Commonwealth No. Depressed, severely and genuinely — but depression is not psychosis. There was no mania and no hypomania, so no bipolar diagnosis, and a commanding voice heard once and never before is not how psychosis presents. Defense Yes. Bipolar disorder with postpartum psychosis, in a woman five months into a collapse nobody treating her had correctly identified. On the day itself she was frankly psychotic and acting on it. Court Not resolved. This is the question the jury could not answer. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Commonwealth The argument A major depressive episode explains everything in the record without requiring psychosis. The bipolar diagnosis was constructed after the fact, by experts retained for the defense, out of material the treating clinicians had already seen and read differently. Rests on Three forensic experts called in rebuttal; the absence of any contemporaneous clinical note recording psychotic symptoms; the singularity of the reported voice. Tr. Days 18, 19, 20, 21 Authority None needed. This is a pure question of fact for the jury. Where it is weak Postpartum psychosis is known to be episodic, to fluctuate, and to be concealed by those experiencing it — which makes its absence from a clinical note weaker evidence than it first appears. Defense The argument The illness was there and was missed. Her own notebooks track the deterioration in real time, and the handwriting degrades with it. What the clinicians did not see is a fact about the clinicians. Rests on Two expert witnesses, one of them among the more experienced forensic psychiatrists in the field; the notebooks; the testimony of her family; the sheer implausibility of the act as a rational one. Tr. Days 15, 16, 17, 18 Authority None needed, and none available — the legal test does not require a recognized diagnosis at all. Where it is weak Both defense experts were retained and examined her long after the event. Neither saw her on or near January 24; the people who did, did not describe what the experts concluded. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Did she have a mental disease or defect on January 24? The Commonwealth must prove she did not. Commonwealth Nobody treating her recorded psychosis, and she denied homicidal thoughts the day before. Commonwealth The contemporaneous record is the best evidence of her state, and it is silent. Defense A record kept by people who were not looking for psychosis is silent either way. Defense The act itself is evidence. No account of it as a rational choice survives contact with the facts. Where it lands Nowhere. Eleven jurors reportedly accepted the defense account and one did not, which under the law is the same as none of them accepting it.
Does the planning show she knew what she was doing?

Commonwealth Yes. She chose the place, the method and the moment, and she sent her husband out of the house to create the moment. Those are decisions, made in sequence, by someone tracking what she was doing. Defense No. Sequencing is not sanity. Psychosis does not remove the ability to act in order; it removes the ability to understand what the order is for. A delusion can be executed methodically and still be a delusion. Court Not resolved. Put to the jury as a question of fact. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Commonwealth The argument Every step narrows the alternatives deliberately. The basement rather than anywhere else. Exercise bands rather than anything at hand. A takeout order and a prescription that put the one other adult in the house on the road for an hour. Rests on The phone records and call timings; the scene; the sequence of that afternoon reconstructed minute by minute in the warrant affidavits and again at trial. Authority The instruction permits the jury to consider conduct before and after the act in deciding capacity. Where it is weak It proves organization, which nobody disputes. The legal test is not organization but appreciation and control, and the Commonwealth has to reach those separately. Defense The argument The same facts read the other way. A woman intending to die that afternoon, convinced her children could not survive without her, would do exactly these things in exactly this order. The planning is evidence of the delusion’s content, not of its absence. Rests on Expert evidence on how postpartum psychosis presents; the fact that she made no attempt to escape, conceal or explain; the near-fatal injuries she inflicted on herself within minutes. Authority Mass. Model Jury Instr. 9.200 — “appreciate” means to understand, not merely to know. Where it is weak It is unfalsifiable in the shape it is usually put. If order is consistent with psychosis and disorder is too, the argument stops doing work and the jury is left with the experts. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Did she retain substantial capacity to appreciate wrongfulness and to conform her conduct? Commonwealth She made a sequence of choices that only make sense if she understood what she was doing. Defense Understanding the mechanics is knowing. The instruction requires appreciating, which is more. Commonwealth Removing the only witness who could stop her shows she knew it was wrong. Defense Or shows only that she knew he would stop her, which is not the same thing. Where it lands Unresolved, and this is the gap the closing arguments were really fought over.
What do the treating clinicians’ records establish?

Commonwealth That the professionals who actually saw her in the months and days beforehand saw no psychosis, and recorded none. She denied homicidal thoughts repeatedly, including at a virtual appointment the day before. Defense That she was misdiagnosed, medicated on a moving target, and treated by people who never spoke to one another. The records show the failure of her care, not the absence of her illness. Court Not resolved. The same evidence now underpins civil suits in Norfolk County. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Commonwealth The argument Clinical records made at the time, by people with no stake in the outcome, beat expert reconstruction made years later by people retained to reach a conclusion. Rests on The testimony of her psychiatrist across two days and her nurse practitioner across a third — the single largest block of evidence in the trial. Tr. Days 9, 10, 11 Authority Ordinary weight-of-evidence reasoning; no legal rule is in play. Where it is weak Both witnesses testified they relied on Clancy to tell them how her other treatment was going, and one did not know the other was still treating her. That damages the records as a record of anything but what she chose to report. Defense The argument A patient reporting her own symptoms to two prescribers who are not talking to each other is not being monitored. The notes are a record of an uncoordinated treatment, and cannot bear the weight the Commonwealth puts on their silence. Rests on Admissions drawn out on cross: reliance on the patient for updates, no request for complete records, no contact between prescribers. Tr. Days 9, 10, 11 Authority None. It is an attack on weight, not admissibility. Where it is weak It cuts both ways. If she concealed symptoms from her clinicians, she was capable of judging what to conceal — which is a point about capacity, and the Commonwealth made it. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test How much does the clinical silence prove? Commonwealth Trained professionals saw her and found nothing to record. Defense They were not looking, were not coordinating, and were relying on her to tell them. Commonwealth Concealment implies judgment, and judgment implies capacity. Defense Concealment of shame is a symptom, not a demonstration of insight. Where it lands Unresolved here, and being litigated again in the civil courts on the opposite assumption.

Commonwealth Argued both ways at different points. That the cuts to her neck and wrists were superficial and not bleeding, and that she may have slid rather than jumped — and elsewhere, that the attempt was sincere and she killed the children first because she would not leave them behind. Defense Unambiguously real. She went out of a second-story window and broke her back. She is paralyzed. The suicide was the plan, and the children died because the delusion made them part of it. Court Not resolved. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Commonwealth The argument The injuries she inflicted with the knife were not consistent with a serious attempt, and the fall is open to an account other than a jump. Rests on The observations of first responders and the emergency clinicians who treated her; the physical evidence at the window. Authority None. Pure fact. Where it is weak The two positions are in tension. A prosecution that argues the attempt was staged, and also that it was sincere and motivated the killings, gives the jury a choice of theories rather than one. It was the sharpest criticism made of the Commonwealth’s presentation. Defense The argument Nothing about the outcome is equivocal. She sustained spinal injuries that ended her ability to walk, within minutes of the deaths, in a house she knew her husband was about to return to. Rests on Her injuries; the timing; the absence of any attempt to leave, conceal or account for what had happened. Authority None. Where it is weak A genuine suicide attempt is consistent with despair as well as with psychosis, and despair is not a defense. The attempt does not by itself reach the legal test. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Does the suicide attempt tell the jury anything about capacity? Defense It establishes that she was not acting to benefit herself, which removes the ordinary motive analysis. Commonwealth Staged, it is consciousness of guilt. Defense Real, and it is the one part of the plan that went as intended. Where it lands Unresolved — and the Commonwealth having argued both branches at different moments made it harder, not easier, to resolve.
Was the investigation sound enough to rely on?

Commonwealth Eleven warrants, a scene processed thoroughly, DNA from the bands, and more than eighty witnesses. Whatever the defense says about individual gaps, the facts it complains about were never the facts in dispute. Defense Investigators settled on a conclusion early and stopped testing it. The affidavits asserted things they never substantiated, a key device sat unexamined for two years, and the gaps run in one direction. Court Declined to instruct the jury that it could acquit on the basis of a faulty investigation. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Commonwealth The argument The defense concedes the conduct. An attack on the investigation of a set of facts nobody contests cannot bear on the only question the jury has to answer. Rests on The scope of the forensic work; the concession itself, offered in writing in April 2026. Authority The judge’s refusal of the faulty-investigation instruction. Where it is weak Credibility is not compartmentalized. A jury told the affidavits asserted something six times that the Commonwealth’s own examiner could not find may discount other things it is told. Defense The argument The clearest instance is the assertion that she was “researching ways to kill.” It appears in six warrant applications in identical words, each time as the reason to search one more device. Nothing in 299 pages supports it. Rests on The affidavits themselves, and the cross-examination of the Commonwealth’s forensic examiner, who agreed there were no such searches and had encountered none. Search warrant affidavits ¶¶40, 42, repeated at pp. 105, 139, 173, 208, 236, 264; Tr. Day 13 Authority Advanced again in September 2026 as part of the Rule 25 motion, which was denied on October 1. Where it is weak A warrant affidavit is not evidence and was never put to the jury as evidence. The point is real but it is aimed at a document the jury was not asked to believe. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Can the quality of the investigation reach a case where the conduct is conceded? Defense An investigation that asserts what it cannot support should not be trusted on what it can. Commonwealth The disputed question is clinical, and no amount of police work was ever going to settle it. Where it lands The instruction was refused, so it reached the jury as argument only. It came back before the judge as a sufficiency point in September 2026 and failed there too.
Did the Commonwealth carry a burden it may not have known it had?

Commonwealth Yes. The evidence of deliberate, sequenced choices, combined with an unbroken clinical record showing no psychosis, proves beyond a reasonable doubt that she appreciated what she was doing and could have done otherwise. Defense No, and it is not close. On a question this contested, with qualified experts on both sides, a jury cannot be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of a proposition about someone else’s mind. That is what the Rule 25 motion says. Court Denied on October 1, 2026. The evidence was enough to go to a jury, and the question of her mind was the jury’s to answer. Detail the argument, what it rests on, where it is weak Commonwealth The argument Sufficiency is a low bar. The question is not whether the jury agreed but whether a rational juror could have convicted on the evidence, and eleven jurors reaching the opposite view does not answer it. Rests on Three rebuttal experts; the treating records; the conduct on the day. Authority Mass. R. Crim. P. 25, and the ordinary standard for a required finding. The judge applied it on October 1, 2026, and found the evidence sufficient. Where it is weak Nothing legally. Practically, a hung jury after thirty-eight hours is an awkward platform from which to argue the case was clear. Defense The argument The Commonwealth had to disprove a mental disease or defect, or prove capacity retained on both prongs. It did neither to the standard required, and the physical evidence it leaned on — the bands, the DNA, the fingerprint work — does not speak to her mind at all. Rests on The Rule 25 motion argued on September 29, 2026. Authority Mass. R. Crim. P. 25; Mass. Model Jury Instr. 9.200. Where it is weak Rule 25 asks whether a rational juror could convict, not whether this jury did. One juror who would have is awkward for the motion, and the Commonwealth will say so. Logic chain how the reasoning runs, and where it breaks Test Could a rational juror have found criminal responsibility proved beyond a reasonable doubt? Defense No. Qualified experts divided, and division at that level is reasonable doubt by definition. Commonwealth Expert disagreement is ordinary and juries resolve it every day. Defense Not when the burden of disproof sits on the side with the weaker experts. Where it lands Decided against the defense on October 1, 2026. The case can be tried again unless the double jeopardy motion succeeds. That was argued on November 2 and hasn’t been decided, and the next hearing is November 16. There is no retrial date yet. The judge has suggested March 2027, and the defense, which said in September it could not be ready before June, now asks for a trial this spring.
